text: How many numbers are in the list [IMAGE: images/7d64adc006e122e3c4100980c2bb9d8e.png]
solution:
Solution for Problem 1.1: Obviously, there are 18 numbers.
 □

That was pretty easy. The counting was already done for us!

Many other counting problems can be reduced to this type of counting.

text: How many numbers are in the list [IMAGE: images/b10896058b40aa80570fd5b0460be359.png]In words, we could ask this problem as “How many numbers are there between 7 and 29 inclusive?” (**Inclusive** means that we include the 7 and the 29 in our count.)
solution:
Solution for Problem 1.2: We could just count them from left to right and find that there are 23 numbers. However, a more clever way to approach this problem is to convert this problem into a problem like Problem 1.1, by subtracting 6 from every number in our list: [IMAGE: images/966f035d9714275445fa670bd30d0521.png]We know how to count the new list! There are 23 items in the list. So, there are 23 items in our original list.
 □

This problem illustrates a very important problem solving idea.

[ICONBOX:concept:Concept]
When presented with a complicated problem, try to reduce or simplify it to a simpler problem that you know how to solve.
[/ICONBOX]

You may also notice that in Problem 1.2, we found that there are $29 - 7 + 1 = 23$ numbers from 7 to 29, inclusive. Perhaps such a formula holds for any two numbers.

text: Given two positive numbers $\color[rgb]{1,1,1}a$ and $\color[rgb]{1,1,1}b$, with $\color[rgb]{1,1,1}b > a$, find a formula for how many numbers there are between $\color[rgb]{1,1,1}a$ and $\color[rgb]{1,1,1}b$ inclusive.
solution:
Solution for Problem 1.3: We can subtract $a-1$ from our list of numbers from $a$ to $b$ to get a list of numbers starting at 1: [IMAGE: images/99c04ebd46739ba7e2be9178155bf93a.png]Our new list then has $b-a+1$ numbers in it, so our old list does too. So the answer is $b-a+1$.
 □

text: How many multiples of 3 are between 62 and 215?
solution:
Solution for Problem 1.4: We see that $\frac{62}{3} = 20\frac23$, so the smallest multiple of 3 in our list is $3 \times 21 = 63$. Similarly, $\frac{215}{3} = 71\frac23$, so the largest multiple of 3 in our list is $3 \times 71=213$. So our list is [IMAGE: images/2b579a886a3c0538e5a0273876b6432a.png]To convert it into a list that we know how to count, we can divide our list by 3: [IMAGE: images/91507be024248749eb3af8768b23563b.png]We know how to count this list! Subtracting 20 from each number in the list gives [IMAGE: images/36c3883409b3b148df9101b8035c40d9.png]So there are 51 numbers in the list.
 □

You might have been tempted to use a little shortcut for Problem 1.4:

[ICONBOX:bogus:Bogus Solution]
We can just compute [IMAGE: images/af253a4d76e5528d760bc9d1e6af09eb.png]to see there are 51 numbers in the list.
[/ICONBOX]

But that “shortcut” doesn’t always work very well, as we can see in the next problem:

text:
(a) How many multiples of 10 are between 9 and 101?
(b) How many multiples of 10 are between 11 and 103?
(c) We know that $\color[rgb]{1,1,1}101-9 = 103-11 = 92$, so shouldn’t your answers to (a) and (b) be the same? Why aren’t they?
solution:
Solution for Problem 1.5: For this problem, it’s easy enough to just list the multiples of 10.
(a) Our list is [IMAGE: images/c41ce04d026781aaf9aca08384f12380.png]so there are 10 multiples.
(b) Our list is [IMAGE: images/9fb9a24eb57849d5326764b253f13cef.png]so there are 9 multiples.
(c) The reason these answers are different is because the “shortcut” solution doesn’t work! You can’t count the number of multiples of 10 simply by calculating [IMAGE: images/49ec104fedee061480c3429332c2b5f8.png]How would you know whether the answer is 9 or 10?
 □

[ICONBOX:warning:WARNING!!]
Beware of quick shortcuts! (Unless you are absolutely certain that your “shortcut” works.)
[/ICONBOX]

text: How many 4-digit numbers are perfect cubes?
solution:
Solution for Problem 1.6: Clearly we don’t want to try to solve this problem by testing each 4-digit number to see if it’s a perfect cube–that would take forever! Instead, if we can find the smallest and biggest numbers in our list, maybe we can find a convenient way to count all the numbers in between.
The smallest 4-digit perfect cube is $1000 = 10^3$.
The largest 4-digit perfect cube is a little harder to find. This requires a bit of experimentation. We can start by noting that $20^3 = 8000$, and then we can use trial and error: [IMAGE: images/526e5fc14a057ee2281b93078551a9a8.png]So $9261=21^3$ is the largest 4-digit cube. Therefore our list is [IMAGE: images/18a96168bff7e6db39f473f91adbe49d.png]But there’s a much better way that we can write this list. Write it as [IMAGE: images/ece814f52d36e9907046c73ad7ac8038.png]Clearly the number of numbers in the list above is the same as the number of numbers in the list below: [IMAGE: images/40b99e9e7d8f5c67bcb381131c87183c.png]There are 12 numbers in this list, so 12 is our answer.
 □
